bull_bear.body:
- Large player in domestic Urea production
- Pan-India distribution and sales network, leveraged for trading and other businesses
- Multi-product company with well established "Kisan" brand (except for subsidised fertilizers)
- Majority equity held by Government of India (74.71% through the President of India), a Central Public Sector Undertaking under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers
- Three plants located in the most intensive fertilizer-consuming states, i.e. Punjab and Haryana
- Manufacturing facilities for industrial products
- Well established eco-system for seed production and sale, including its own flagship Seed Multiplication Programme
- Strong presence in the Southern market after commissioning of RFCL
- Adequate infrastructure for future expansion/sharing
- Skilled and experienced workforce
- Direct-to-farmer reach through NFL Direct Sales Centers at 34 locations under "Kisan Dhan – Seedhe Kisan Tak"
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Tightening Target Energy Norms under New Urea Policy (NUP)-2015 — Management flags this as a major risk with severe financial impact: tightening of energy norms has reduced operational profit from the urea manufacturing business, mainly at the Vijaipur-I unit, and further reduction in energy norms shall make operations unviable. NFL has already spent more than Rs 1000 crore to meet revised norms, and the Vijaipur-I norm extension carries a 35% penalty on the difference between revised and tentative norms. Norms are under further review, with DoF revising the New Energy Norms applicable from 01.04.2025 to 31.03.2028.
- Natural gas / RLNG supply constraints due to geopolitical factors — Identified by the Risk Assessment and Risk Management Committees as a major risk with severe financial impact on production. Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East disrupted international prices of natural gas, ammonia, urea and phosphatic fertilizers and raised freight and logistics costs, and lack of availability of domestic gas with an increasing trend in RLNG prices adversely impacts urea manufacturers' profitability.
- Dependence on Government subsidy and delayed subsidy receipts — Urea is sold at a GoI-controlled price and the business depends on subsidy; delay in receipt of subsidy leads to higher interest cost. Implementation of DBT changed subsidy payment from supply to sale, aggravating the working capital problem. Short-term borrowings rose to Rs 3,959.25 crore as at 31.03.2026 from Rs 1,995.77 crore a year earlier, mainly due to the high cost of imported P&K fertilizers.
- Low operating margins in Urea due to a tightly regulated pricing environment — Listed as both a weakness and a risk. Urea MRP is fixed by GoI and is highly inadequate relative to current cost of production or imported price; the Government has not yet considered raising the minimum fixed cost of Rs 2,300 per tonne of Urea, which is affecting the viability of some units including Vijaipur-I. Deletion of the minimum fixed cost provision retrospectively w.e.f. 02.04.2014 for Vijaipur-I is separately flagged.
- Old, smaller and less energy-efficient plants at Bathinda, Nangal and Panipat — These plants consume higher energy than new and large-capacity plants, structurally disadvantaging them against the tightening energy norms and raising the cost of production.
- Lack of internal resources (funds) for future investment — Explicitly flagged in MD&A Risk & Concerns; constrains NFL's ability to fund equity participation in domestic and overseas fertilizer companies and its own expansion programme at a time when the debt equity ratio has risen to 1.39:1 as on 31.03.2026 from 0.72:1.
- Manpower shortfall from massive retirements and manpower rationalisation — MD&A lists recruitment of manpower to meet the shortfall arising out of massive retirements and future growth, and rationalisation of manpower, as risks and concerns; permanent employee turnover was 13.72% in FY 2025-26.
- Hazardous-process safety and environmental compliance exposure — The chemical fertilizer industry operates in a hazardous environment and faces risks related to health, safety and environment in addition to general business and financial risks; the Company handles hazardous substances such as liquid ammonia and chlorine gas and carries Extended Producer Responsibility obligations for roughly 16,000 metric tonnes of plastic waste annually under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016.
- Concentration in Urea and in the domestic Indian market, with adverse agro-climatic and import-price exposure — Manufactured Urea still contributes 59.66% of gross sales and exports are Nil, so the business is exposed to an adverse fertilizer demand-supply scenario from adverse agro-climatic conditions, volatility in prices of imported fertilizers and industrial products, and the threat of decontrol of Urea.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body: NFL manufactures and sells fertilizer-grade Urea, Bentonite Sulphur and bio-fertilizers, and also produces allied industrial products such as Nitric Acid, Ammonium Nitrate, Sodium Nitrate and Nitrite from its Nangal Unit. Alongside manufacturing, it imports and sells fertilizers such as DAP, MoP and NPKs and trades domestic agro-inputs including certified seeds, agrochemicals, City Compost, SSP, Potash Derived from Molasses (PDM), Fermented Organic Manure (FOM) and Seaweed Granules through a vast dealer network under a single-window concept. Its customers are farmers, supplied through a wholesale dealer network comprising private, government and institutional channels, with no exports.

- **Traded Imported Fertilizers (under NBS):** Urea (imported), DAP, MoP, APS, NPK, Water Soluble Fertilizer including Calcium Nitrate

outlook.body:
- Maximise Urea production in an energy-efficient manner, keeping consumption within the Target Energy Norms under NUP-2015
- Maximise production of industrial products including Ammonium Nitrate and Nitric Acid
- Maximise production of Bentonite Sulphur and bio-fertilizers
- Produce new products such as Sulphur Coated Urea (Urea Gold) and agro-chemicals
- Import and sell fertilizers such as Urea, DAP, MoP, complex fertilizers and water soluble fertilizer including Calcium Nitrate
- Expand domestic trading of agro products — pesticides, weedicides, compost, water soluble fertilizers, Calcium Nitrate, SSP, PDM and FOM
- Shift the mix away from subsidised Urea towards non-subsidised products to enhance long-term profitability and reduce reliance on Urea
- Leverage the existing pan-India marketing network for trading and other businesses
- Market Urea manufactured by RFCL and take equity participation in fertilizer companies domestic and abroad
- Expand direct-to-farmer distribution through NFL Direct Sales Centers under the banner "Kisan Dhan – Seedhe Kisan Tak", presently at 34 locations, to reduce dependency on intermediaries
- Pursue global collaborations for fertilizer resource security, including the feasibility study with Uralchem JSC, RCF and IPL for a urea facility in Russia
- Implement phase-wise energy-saving schemes recommended by Topsoe and Saipem across Nangal, Bathinda, Panipat and Vijaipur-I & II units
- Adopt green energy through rooftop solar PV plants at manufacturing units
- Rationalise manpower and recruit to meet the shortfall arising from retirements and future growth
- Digitalisation through the ERP system implemented at all levels to integrate business functions
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: NFL's largest expansion is the Namrup-IV brownfield Ammonia-Urea complex at Namrup, Assam, taken forward through the joint venture company Assam Valley Fertilizer and Chemical Company Limited (AVFCCL) incorporated on 25.07.2025 with the Government of Assam (40%), NFL (18%), OIL (18%), HURL (13%) and BVFCL (11%); the plant will have annual urea production capacity of 12.7 LMT, tentative CAPEX of Rs 10,601.40 crore, NFL equity contribution of around Rs 572.45 crore, and a tentative schedule of 48 months to mechanical completion and commissioning. Domestically, NFL is planning a 25,000 MTPA Bentonite Sulphur plant at its Vijaipur Unit at an estimated cost of Rs 104.03 crore with an implementation period of about 14 months, and — following Department of Fertilizers direction — two commercial-scale Sulphur Coated Urea (Urea Gold) plants of 250 MTPD at Nangal and 300 MTPD at Vijaipur, with PDIL being lined up as Project Management Consultant. Completed or in-progress smaller projects include the Agro-chemical plant at Bathinda at an approximate cost of Rs 12.57 crore (production commenced from three of five trains, one under rectification and one under completion by the contractor), the 5,000 MTPA Urea Gold R&D plants at Panipat and Nangal costing Rs 3.43 crore and Rs 6.52 crore respectively (desired R&D results not achieved; Nangal under modification and Panipat equipment planned for use as spares at Nangal), the doubling of the Vijaipur bio-fertilizer plant from 700 MTPA to 1,400 MTPA during FY 2025-26, and the completed ERP implementation. On renewables, a 1500 kWp grid-connected rooftop Solar PV plant at Panipat (total capex Rs 6.67 crore including GST) has slipped from December 2025 to an expected August 2026 completion, and rooftop solar plants of 1735 kWp, 600 kWp and 1220 kWp are planned at Nangal, Bathinda and Vijaipur respectively; a 300 KW rooftop solar plant already operates at Vijaipur. Integrated energy-saving projects continue: Topsoe-recommended schemes are being implemented phase-wise starting with the synthesis gas compressor and steam turbine drive revamp at Nangal, Bathinda and Panipat, while Saipem-recommended schemes for Vijaipur-I & II remain to be implemented. Overseas, NFL with RCF and Indian Potash Limited has a strategic collaboration with Uralchem JSC to explore a 2 million MT per annum urea facility in Russia, currently at feasibility-study stage. The Directors' Report states CAPEX achievement of Rs 247 crore excluding capital work in progress in 2025-26.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Company envisages growth in its top and bottom line by adopting business strategies of maximising urea and industrial product output, new products and expanded agro-input trading
- The Indian fertilizer market is expected to grow at 3-4% annually over the next five years, with the strongest growth likely in nano fertilizers, bio-fertilizers, micronutrients and specialty nutrient products
- The Indian fertilizer industry is expected to maintain a steady growth trajectory over the medium to long term, supported by rising agricultural demand, government policy support, increasing adoption of specialty and nano fertilizers and efforts towards self-reliance
- Domestic fertilizer demand remained robust supported by favourable monsoon conditions; urea continued to be the most consumed fertilizer, creating opportunities for domestic producers
- Domestic producers are strategically positioned to benefit from sustained demand growth and the Government's emphasis on fertilizer security
- Continued subsidy support ensured affordability to farmers, maintained demand stability and supported the financial sustainability of fertilizer manufacturers; the FY 2025-26 revised estimate for fertilizer subsidy rose to approximately Rs 1,86,460 crore
- Import dependence for phosphatic and potassic nutrients is likely to continue, making global commodity prices and supply-chain dynamics important determinants of industry performance
- Near-term global outlook is characterised by price volatility, geopolitical risks and supply-chain uncertainties; Middle East tensions affected prices of natural gas, ammonia, urea and phosphatic fertilizers and raised freight and logistics costs
- Progressive strategic shift has changed the gross sale composition — manufactured Urea down to 59.66% of sales from 94.49% in 2015-16, with other products at 40.34%
- Government policies promoting self-reliance, nano fertilizers and balanced nutrient usage are expected to influence future demand patterns; over the long term nano fertilizers may partially reduce conventional fertilizer demand growth
- Efficiency of existing Indian fertilizer plants is already comparable to the best in the world, so there is little scope for further energy efficiency improvement from plant modifications
- Low operating margins in Urea due to a tight regulatory environment, and tightening energy norms under NUP-2015, constrain profitability of urea manufacturing

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: National Fertilizers Limited is a Government of India-controlled central public sector fertilizer company operating five gas-based Urea plants, with the Government of India holding 74.71% of its paid-up share capital.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: NFL manufactures and sells fertilizer-grade Urea, Bentonite Sulphur and bio-fertilizers, and also produces allied industrial products such as Nitric Acid, Ammonium Nitrate, Sodium Nitrate and Nitrite from its Nangal Unit. Alongside manufacturing, it imports and sells fertilizers such as DAP, MoP and NPKs and trades domestic agro-inputs including certified seeds, agrochemicals, City Compost, SSP, Potash Derived from Molasses (PDM), Fermented Organic Manure (FOM) and Seaweed Granules through a vast dealer network under a single-window concept. Its customers are farmers, supplied through a wholesale dealer network comprising private, government and institutional channels, with no exports.

group_structure.title: Group structure (subsidiaries / JV / related parties)
group_structure.body:
- Urvarak Videsh Limited (UVL) — associate: Associate company with 33.33% of shares held by NFL; also listed as a related party in the Ind AS-24 disclosure
- Ramagundam Fertilizers and Chemicals Limited (RFCL) — associate: Associate company with 26.00% of shares held by NFL; significant influence due to control; NFL markets urea and purchases ammonia from RFCL and shares marketing and transportation services with it
- Assam Valley Fertilizer and Chemical Company Limited (AVFCCL) — associate: Joint venture company incorporated 25.07.2025 among the Government of Assam (40%), NFL (18%), OIL (18%), HURL (13%) and BVFCL (11%) to set up the Namrup-IV brownfield Ammonia-Urea complex at Namrup, Assam; NFL holds 20.24% per the BRSR and AOC-1 disclosure and it is yet to commence operations
- NFL Employees Provident Fund Trust — related party: Post-employment benefit plan of the Company
- NFL Employees Defined Contribution Super Annuation Trust — related party: Post-employment benefit plan of the Company
- NFL Employees Group Gratuity Trust — related party: Post-employment benefit plan of the Company
- Government of India / other Government-related entities — related party: Entities under the control of the same government; the Company is a CPSU under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, with transactions including purchase of fuel (coal, gas) and other services carried out at market terms through transparent price discovery against open tenders

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Manufactured Fertilizers:** Urea, Bentonite Sulphur, Bio-Fertilizers, Urea Gold (Sulphur Coated Urea)
- **Manufactured Chemicals / Industrial Products:** Nitric Acid, Ammonium Nitrate, Sodium Nitrate, Sodium Nitrite, Agro Chemicals
- **Traded Imported Fertilizers (under NBS):** Urea (imported), DAP, MoP, APS, NPK, Water Soluble Fertilizer including Calcium Nitrate
- **Others / Domestic Traded Agro-Inputs:** Certified Seeds, Agrochemicals / Pesticides, City Compost, SSP, Potash Derived from Molasses (PDM), Fermented Organic Manure (FOM), Seaweed Granules, Micronutrients

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- Indian agriculture — farmers served through wholesale dealer network (private, government and institutional)
- Domestic market only; exports are Nil
- Operations across 23 states in India, with plants concentrated in Punjab, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh
- Strong presence in the Southern market after commissioning of RFCL
- Industrial customers for Nitric Acid, Ammonium Nitrate and Sodium Nitrate

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Company envisages growth in its top and bottom line by adopting business strategies of maximising urea and industrial product output, new products and expanded agro-input trading
- The Indian fertilizer market is expected to grow at 3-4% annually over the next five years, with the strongest growth likely in nano fertilizers, bio-fertilizers, micronutrients and specialty nutrient products
- The Indian fertilizer industry is expected to maintain a steady growth trajectory over the medium to long term, supported by rising agricultural demand, government policy support, increasing adoption of specialty and nano fertilizers and efforts towards self-reliance
- Domestic fertilizer demand remained robust supported by favourable monsoon conditions; urea continued to be the most consumed fertilizer, creating opportunities for domestic producers
- Domestic producers are strategically positioned to benefit from sustained demand growth and the Government's emphasis on fertilizer security
- Continued subsidy support ensured affordability to farmers, maintained demand stability and supported the financial sustainability of fertilizer manufacturers; the FY 2025-26 revised estimate for fertilizer subsidy rose to approximately Rs 1,86,460 crore
- Import dependence for phosphatic and potassic nutrients is likely to continue, making global commodity prices and supply-chain dynamics important determinants of industry performance
- Near-term global outlook is characterised by price volatility, geopolitical risks and supply-chain uncertainties; Middle East tensions affected prices of natural gas, ammonia, urea and phosphatic fertilizers and raised freight and logistics costs
- Progressive strategic shift has changed the gross sale composition — manufactured Urea down to 59.66% of sales from 94.49% in 2015-16, with other products at 40.34%
- Government policies promoting self-reliance, nano fertilizers and balanced nutrient usage are expected to influence future demand patterns; over the long term nano fertilizers may partially reduce conventional fertilizer demand growth
- Efficiency of existing Indian fertilizer plants is already comparable to the best in the world, so there is little scope for further energy efficiency improvement from plant modifications
- Low operating margins in Urea due to a tight regulatory environment, and tightening energy norms under NUP-2015, constrain profitability of urea manufacturing

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Maximise Urea production in an energy-efficient manner, keeping consumption within the Target Energy Norms under NUP-2015
- Maximise production of industrial products including Ammonium Nitrate and Nitric Acid
- Maximise production of Bentonite Sulphur and bio-fertilizers
- Produce new products such as Sulphur Coated Urea (Urea Gold) and agro-chemicals
- Import and sell fertilizers such as Urea, DAP, MoP, complex fertilizers and water soluble fertilizer including Calcium Nitrate
- Expand domestic trading of agro products — pesticides, weedicides, compost, water soluble fertilizers, Calcium Nitrate, SSP, PDM and FOM
- Shift the mix away from subsidised Urea towards non-subsidised products to enhance long-term profitability and reduce reliance on Urea
- Leverage the existing pan-India marketing network for trading and other businesses
- Market Urea manufactured by RFCL and take equity participation in fertilizer companies domestic and abroad
- Expand direct-to-farmer distribution through NFL Direct Sales Centers under the banner "Kisan Dhan – Seedhe Kisan Tak", presently at 34 locations, to reduce dependency on intermediaries
- Pursue global collaborations for fertilizer resource security, including the feasibility study with Uralchem JSC, RCF and IPL for a urea facility in Russia
- Implement phase-wise energy-saving schemes recommended by Topsoe and Saipem across Nangal, Bathinda, Panipat and Vijaipur-I & II units
- Adopt green energy through rooftop solar PV plants at manufacturing units
- Rationalise manpower and recruit to meet the shortfall arising from retirements and future growth
- Digitalisation through the ERP system implemented at all levels to integrate business functions

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: NFL's largest expansion is the Namrup-IV brownfield Ammonia-Urea complex at Namrup, Assam, taken forward through the joint venture company Assam Valley Fertilizer and Chemical Company Limited (AVFCCL) incorporated on 25.07.2025 with the Government of Assam (40%), NFL (18%), OIL (18%), HURL (13%) and BVFCL (11%); the plant will have annual urea production capacity of 12.7 LMT, tentative CAPEX of Rs 10,601.40 crore, NFL equity contribution of around Rs 572.45 crore, and a tentative schedule of 48 months to mechanical completion and commissioning. Domestically, NFL is planning a 25,000 MTPA Bentonite Sulphur plant at its Vijaipur Unit at an estimated cost of Rs 104.03 crore with an implementation period of about 14 months, and — following Department of Fertilizers direction — two commercial-scale Sulphur Coated Urea (Urea Gold) plants of 250 MTPD at Nangal and 300 MTPD at Vijaipur, with PDIL being lined up as Project Management Consultant. Completed or in-progress smaller projects include the Agro-chemical plant at Bathinda at an approximate cost of Rs 12.57 crore (production commenced from three of five trains, one under rectification and one under completion by the contractor), the 5,000 MTPA Urea Gold R&D plants at Panipat and Nangal costing Rs 3.43 crore and Rs 6.52 crore respectively (desired R&D results not achieved; Nangal under modification and Panipat equipment planned for use as spares at Nangal), the doubling of the Vijaipur bio-fertilizer plant from 700 MTPA to 1,400 MTPA during FY 2025-26, and the completed ERP implementation. On renewables, a 1500 kWp grid-connected rooftop Solar PV plant at Panipat (total capex Rs 6.67 crore including GST) has slipped from December 2025 to an expected August 2026 completion, and rooftop solar plants of 1735 kWp, 600 kWp and 1220 kWp are planned at Nangal, Bathinda and Vijaipur respectively; a 300 KW rooftop solar plant already operates at Vijaipur. Integrated energy-saving projects continue: Topsoe-recommended schemes are being implemented phase-wise starting with the synthesis gas compressor and steam turbine drive revamp at Nangal, Bathinda and Panipat, while Saipem-recommended schemes for Vijaipur-I & II remain to be implemented. Overseas, NFL with RCF and Indian Potash Limited has a strategic collaboration with Uralchem JSC to explore a 2 million MT per annum urea facility in Russia, currently at feasibility-study stage. The Directors' Report states CAPEX achievement of Rs 247 crore excluding capital work in progress in 2025-26.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Large player in domestic Urea production
- Pan-India distribution and sales network, leveraged for trading and other businesses
- Multi-product company with well established "Kisan" brand (except for subsidised fertilizers)
- Majority equity held by Government of India (74.71% through the President of India), a Central Public Sector Undertaking under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers
- Three plants located in the most intensive fertilizer-consuming states, i.e. Punjab and Haryana
- Manufacturing facilities for industrial products
- Well established eco-system for seed production and sale, including its own flagship Seed Multiplication Programme
- Strong presence in the Southern market after commissioning of RFCL
- Adequate infrastructure for future expansion/sharing
- Skilled and experienced workforce
- Direct-to-farmer reach through NFL Direct Sales Centers at 34 locations under "Kisan Dhan – Seedhe Kisan Tak"

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Tightening Target Energy Norms under New Urea Policy (NUP)-2015 — Management flags this as a major risk with severe financial impact: tightening of energy norms has reduced operational profit from the urea manufacturing business, mainly at the Vijaipur-I unit, and further reduction in energy norms shall make operations unviable. NFL has already spent more than Rs 1000 crore to meet revised norms, and the Vijaipur-I norm extension carries a 35% penalty on the difference between revised and tentative norms. Norms are under further review, with DoF revising the New Energy Norms applicable from 01.04.2025 to 31.03.2028.
- Natural gas / RLNG supply constraints due to geopolitical factors — Identified by the Risk Assessment and Risk Management Committees as a major risk with severe financial impact on production. Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East disrupted international prices of natural gas, ammonia, urea and phosphatic fertilizers and raised freight and logistics costs, and lack of availability of domestic gas with an increasing trend in RLNG prices adversely impacts urea manufacturers' profitability.
- Dependence on Government subsidy and delayed subsidy receipts — Urea is sold at a GoI-controlled price and the business depends on subsidy; delay in receipt of subsidy leads to higher interest cost. Implementation of DBT changed subsidy payment from supply to sale, aggravating the working capital problem. Short-term borrowings rose to Rs 3,959.25 crore as at 31.03.2026 from Rs 1,995.77 crore a year earlier, mainly due to the high cost of imported P&K fertilizers.
- Low operating margins in Urea due to a tightly regulated pricing environment — Listed as both a weakness and a risk. Urea MRP is fixed by GoI and is highly inadequate relative to current cost of production or imported price; the Government has not yet considered raising the minimum fixed cost of Rs 2,300 per tonne of Urea, which is affecting the viability of some units including Vijaipur-I. Deletion of the minimum fixed cost provision retrospectively w.e.f. 02.04.2014 for Vijaipur-I is separately flagged.
- Old, smaller and less energy-efficient plants at Bathinda, Nangal and Panipat — These plants consume higher energy than new and large-capacity plants, structurally disadvantaging them against the tightening energy norms and raising the cost of production.
- Lack of internal resources (funds) for future investment — Explicitly flagged in MD&A Risk & Concerns; constrains NFL's ability to fund equity participation in domestic and overseas fertilizer companies and its own expansion programme at a time when the debt equity ratio has risen to 1.39:1 as on 31.03.2026 from 0.72:1.
- Manpower shortfall from massive retirements and manpower rationalisation — MD&A lists recruitment of manpower to meet the shortfall arising out of massive retirements and future growth, and rationalisation of manpower, as risks and concerns; permanent employee turnover was 13.72% in FY 2025-26.
- Hazardous-process safety and environmental compliance exposure — The chemical fertilizer industry operates in a hazardous environment and faces risks related to health, safety and environment in addition to general business and financial risks; the Company handles hazardous substances such as liquid ammonia and chlorine gas and carries Extended Producer Responsibility obligations for roughly 16,000 metric tonnes of plastic waste annually under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016.
- Concentration in Urea and in the domestic Indian market, with adverse agro-climatic and import-price exposure — Manufactured Urea still contributes 59.66% of gross sales and exports are Nil, so the business is exposed to an adverse fertilizer demand-supply scenario from adverse agro-climatic conditions, volatility in prices of imported fertilizers and industrial products, and the threat of decontrol of Urea.

themes.title: Fertilizer subsidy & nutrient-policy cycle
themes.need: Fertilizer makers are driven by NBS/urea subsidy policy, gas-pooling and nutrient pricing rather than the crop-protection volume/molecule-launch recovery. Q1FY27's supply-side read comes from MBAPL: revenue roughly flat at INR 416cr with EBITDA +16% and PAT +17% purely on cheap March-bought raw material that management said is now EXHAUSTED, with utilisation only ~43-45% because of raw-material availability rather than demand - SSP sales were +28% and NPK +33% YoY against production down 7%/28%. Its Dhule (Maharashtra) integrated complex commissions +3,30,000 MTPA DAP-NPK plus 99,000 MTPA phosphoric acid in Oct-2026 and a second phase in Oct-2027, framed as a >50% turnover jump toward ~INR 3,500cr revenue and 15.6 lakh MT capacity by FY28; Egypt/Jordan rock-phosphate sourcing (non-Hormuz) insulated it relative to import-dependent peers. Subsidy clarity and gas costs still set the near-term margin.
themes.driver: NBS/urea subsidy policy (the Oct-Mar rate revision), gas-pooling and nutrient pricing; MBAPL's Oct-2026 Dhule commissioning and the utilisation ramp toward ~90%; kharif demand pull-through after a delayed monsoon.
